strengths: The paper targets an important and relevant problem: non-invasive EMG-to-speech generation, with clear potential significance for assistive communication and speech interfaces.

The proposed connection between self-supervised speech representations and EMG-derived articulatory power is interesting, and the linear-probing analysis across HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, and WavLM is a useful way to investigate representational alignment.

The data collection effort appears substantial relative to much prior EMG speech work: 31 electrodes, a large-vocabulary corpus, natural speaking rate, and explicit train/validation/test sentence splits.

The paper gives a reasonably clear high-level pipeline using EMG covariance/power features, CTC prediction of HuBERT units or phonemes, and a pretrained vocoder, and it compares several EMG feature representations.
The ethical statement reports informed consent, deidentification consent, and participant inclusion/exclusion criteria.
weaknesses: The central claim of synthesizing speech from EMG is not adequately supported. The paper reports unit error rate and phoneme error rate, but provides no objective speech-quality, intelligibility, WER/CER, speaker similarity, listening-test, or audio-resynthesis evaluation. Section 6 explicitly states that such evaluation is still ongoing.

The reported decoding performance is still weak: UER around 59% and PER around 41% for the best feature. Without synthesized-audio metrics or comparison to meaningful baselines, it is unclear whether the system produces usable speech.

Reproducibility is currently insufficient. The paper says data and code will be released only upon project completion, and important implementation details are missing, including TDS hyperparameters, training schedules, optimization details, feature windowing specifics, normalization, lag/alignment handling, subject splits, number of runs, and exact evaluation protocol.

The experimental design leaves major confounds unresolved. It is unclear whether train/test splits are sentence-only or also subject/session independent; same-speaker/session leakage could make the task substantially easier. The high linear correlation between audio SSL features and EMG power may also be driven by broad timing, energy, silence/onset structure, or coarticulation rather than the claimed articulatory mechanism.

The paper’s mechanistic interpretation is stronger than the evidence warrants. Showing that H linearly predicts D(E) does not by itself establish that SSL models implicitly encode muscle activations or explain why HuBERT layer 6 works for resynthesis; stronger controls, ablations, lag analyses, statistical tests, and comparisons to simpler acoustic features are needed.

The gesture-clustering analysis is underdeveloped. It uses a separate dataset, only one t-SNE visualization, and k-medoids accuracy, but lacks details on cross-validation, chance definition, subject variability, confidence intervals, and whether clusters generalize across participants.

The paper lacks comparisons to existing EMG-to-speech/silent-speech baselines on the same task or dataset. This makes it hard to judge whether covariance features, SSL-unit prediction, or the proposed architecture improve over established spectrogram or direct phoneme/word recognition methods.

Some claims about addressing prior limitations are premature: the dataset is not yet public, the benchmark is not fully specified, and the system is not evaluated under clinically relevant conditions such as silent articulation, laryngectomy, dysarthria, electrode displacement, or session drift.

Presentation is generally understandable but still draft-like, with placeholder/incomplete IRB text, a blank conflict-of-interest section, formatting issues, and occasional overclaims relative to the results.

strengths: The problem is relevant and potentially important: non-invasive EMG-to-speech interfaces with larger vocabularies and natural speaking rates are well within the scope of ACL/NLP and could have meaningful accessibility impact.

The paper proposes an interpretable representational hypothesis connecting EMG covariance/power features with self-supervised speech representations, and the layer-wise probing across HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, and WavLM is a useful direction.

The dataset, if released as described, would be valuable: approximately 9 hours, 6,800 unique words, 9,660 sentences, and a natural speaking rate would improve on many small-vocabulary EMG/speech-interface settings.
The comparison among EMG feature representations is a reasonable empirical component, and the finding that covariance-based vec(E) and D(E) outperform spectrogram features is potentially interesting.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method synthesizes speech from EMG is not adequately supported. The paper reports UER and PER only, with very high errors, and explicitly states that WER, CER, and perceptual audio-quality evaluation are still continuing work. There is no objective or human evaluation of the generated speech.

The empirical case for acceptance is weak because there are no strong baselines against prior EMG-to-speech methods, no comparison to standard EMG features under comparable architectures beyond the limited feature table, and no demonstration that the synthesized output is intelligible or useful.

The linear-probing claim is overstated. A high correlation from SSL speech features to EMG power does not by itself establish that SSL models encode articulatory mechanisms in the strong sense claimed; alternative explanations such as shared phonetic timing, speaker/session correlations, or audio-derived lexical structure are not controlled for.

Dataset description is incomplete. The manuscript does not clearly state the number of participants for the main 9-hour corpus, whether results are within-subject or cross-subject, how train/test splits avoid subject/session leakage, how audio was recorded, or whether the task is audible speech, silent articulation, or both.

Reproducibility is currently poor. Code and data are promised only upon project completion, and many implementation details are missing: TDS architecture hyperparameters, training setup, optimizer, batch size, augmentation, covariance windowing, epsilon choice, discrete-unit extraction details, vocoder configuration, and decoding procedures.

The methodology has unresolved alignment and timing issues. The paper motivates unknown alignment, but does not explain precisely how EMG frames, audio/SSL features, timestamps, and CTC targets are synchronized or validated, especially given sentence-level click timestamps.

The reported performance is not convincing for a speech-interface contribution. PER of 41.42% for the best feature representation and UER of 58.7% suggest limited decoding quality, yet the paper does not analyze errors, intelligibility, or practical utility.

Several claims are broader than the evidence warrants, including claims about few-shot and zero-shot potential, efficient end-to-end EMG-to-audio generation, and addressing limitations of prior work. These are mostly prospective rather than demonstrated.

The paper reads as unfinished in places: Section 6 describes key evaluations as future work, the conflict-of-interest section appears empty, and the main contribution is positioned around synthesis despite the absence of synthesis evaluation.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: non-invasive EMG-to-speech synthesis, with clear relevance to speech interfaces, assistive communication, and computational modeling of articulatory information in self-supervised speech representations.

The central representational analysis is interesting and relatively well motivated. The finding that self-supervised speech features can linearly predict EMG power with high correlation, and that EMG covariance/power features cluster by articulatory gesture, provides plausible evidence that these representations encode articulatory structure.

The data collection effort appears substantial compared with much prior EMG-to-speech work: the paper describes around 9 hours of natural-rate speech, 6,800 unique words, and train/validation/test splits with held-out sentences. If released as promised, this could be a useful resource.

The paper is generally readable and connects the proposed modeling choices to prior work on HuBERT units, CTC alignment-free decoding, and EMG feature representations. The comparison among vec(E), D(E), and EMG spectrogram features is informative and supports the claim that covariance-based features are useful.
The ethical statement and participant consent discussion are appropriate, and the paper acknowledges practical sources of EMG variability such as electrode displacement and skin conditions.
weaknesses: The strongest claim, EMG-to-speech synthesis, is not adequately evaluated. The paper reports UER and PER, but does not provide objective or human evaluation of synthesized audio quality, intelligibility, WER/CER, speaker similarity, latency, or comparisons to prior EMG-to-speech systems. Section 6 states that such evaluation is still ongoing, which leaves the main application claim under-supported.

Reproducibility is currently limited. The paper says data and code will be released later, but they are not available at submission time. Important implementation details are also missing or underspecified, including TDS architecture hyperparameters, training schedules, optimizer settings, CTC decoding details beyond greedy search, feature windowing/normalization, exact HuBERT quantization setup, number of runs, and participant/session split details.

The experimental evidence is narrower than the framing suggests. The articulatory-gesture clustering experiment is collected separately from the speech corpus, uses a different subset of electrodes, and involves isolated gestures rather than continuous speech articulation; this weakens the inference from gesture separability to full EMG-to-speech synthesis performance.

The paper lacks strong baselines. It compares EMG feature representations within the proposed pipeline, but does not compare against existing EMG-to-speech models, direct phoneme/character recognition baselines, mel-spectrogram prediction, aligned settings, or simpler neural encoders. This makes it difficult to judge the actual contribution over prior work.

The reported downstream performance appears modest: UER remains around 59% even for vec(E), and PER remains around 41%. Without audio intelligibility results or prior-system comparisons, it is unclear whether the synthesized speech is practically useful.

Some claims are phrased more strongly than the evidence supports. For example, the paper argues that SS models implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms and that the layer-6 result explains prior resynthesis performance, but the evidence is correlational and does not rule out confounds from phonetic/acoustic content, coarticulation, timing, or dataset-specific structure.

The dataset description is incomplete. The manuscript clearly states 12 participants for the isolated gesture study, but the main speech corpus participant/session composition is unclear, including whether train/test splits are within-speaker, cross-session, or cross-speaker. This matters greatly for EMG generalization.

Statistical rigor is limited. The paper reports some standard deviations for UER/PER, but does not specify what they are computed over, and does not report significance testing, confidence intervals for the correlation analyses, or robustness to participant/session variability.

The paper would be stronger if it separated a solid Findings-level contribution, such as the dataset plus representational analysis, from the less mature speech synthesis claim. As written, the synthesis component feels preliminary relative to the title and abstract.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored NLP/speech-interface problem: converting orofacial EMG into speech, including a clinically relevant ALS demonstration.

The proposed public datasets are a substantial contribution if released as claimed: about 9 hours/9,660 sentences from a healthy participant, 1 hour/600 sentences from an ALS participant, and a 12-participant articulatory-gesture dataset.

The methodology is clearly motivated: covariance EMG features, probing their relation to self-supervised speech representations, CTC training for unaligned EMG-to-unit/phoneme prediction, and phoneme-guided regularization form a coherent pipeline.

The paper includes useful ablations and diagnostics: covariance vs spectrogram features, D(E) vs vec(E), unit-only vs phoneme-guided decoding, data-size scaling, human WER/PER transcription, MOS ratings, and implementation details in the appendix.

The main empirical trends are consistent and plausible: full covariance vec(E) outperforms spectrogram features, low-dimensional D(E) remains competitive, and phoneme-guided training improves HuBERT-unit decoding.

Reproducibility is better than many papers in this space: the authors provide preprocessing, architecture, optimization, electrode-placement, and evaluation details, and claim code/data/audio release.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are overextended relative to the evidence. The assertion that S3 models implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms is based mainly on linear predictability of EMG power from representations for one healthy participant, which does not rule out correlations with acoustics, phonetic labels, duration, speaker-specific timing, or corpus structure.

The clinical evidence is very limited: only one ALS participant, about one hour of data, no longitudinal evaluation, no electrode-replacement/session-shift study, and no demonstration that the approach generalizes across clinical populations or days.

The main EMG-to-speech results remain preliminary in quality: human WER is high, about 62.6% on DATA_GENERAL and 50.8% on DATA_ALS, so the system is far from functional communication despite moderately high MOS.

Comparisons to prior work are mostly contextual rather than experimental. There is no strong direct baseline on the released data from established EMG-to-speech methods, aligned-audio methods, simpler CTC phoneme/text systems, or modern ASR/LM-assisted decoding under matched conditions.

The use of gTTS-derived HuBERT units from transcripts is reasonable for unaligned training, but it changes the task formulation substantially. It is closer to learning EMG-to-transcript-derived speech units than recovering natural participant speech, and the implications for prosody, speaker identity, and real silent-speech synthesis are not fully characterized.

The phoneme-guided method has possible leakage/overfitting ambiguities: the unit-to-phoneme table is learned using DATA_GENERAL with a reported 0% PER, but it is unclear exactly which splits are used to estimate the conditional table and whether any test-set information enters auxiliary targets or calibration.

The gesture separability analysis is suggestive but not rigorous enough to support broad mechanistic claims: t-SNE is shown for one subject, clustering details are limited, and no cross-subject or held-out-subject validation is reported.

The paper would benefit from clearer statistical reporting beyond one p-value: confidence intervals for human WER/MOS, details of rater protocol and normalization, significance for feature comparisons, and robustness across seeds/splits would strengthen the conclusions.
The claimed reproducibility depends on actual availability of project/code/data links; the manuscript text itself contains placeholders/icons, so the release cannot be verified from the paper alone.

Overall, the work is sound enough for Findings and close to main-conference level because of the dataset and promising formulation, but the evidence is too narrow and the system performance too preliminary for a confident Conference recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: non-invasive EMG-based speech restoration, including a demonstration on an ALS participant silently articulating speech.

The planned release of EMG-to-speech data is a meaningful contribution, especially given the scarcity of public datasets in this area. The healthy-participant corpus is larger and less vocabulary-constrained than much prior EMG-to-speech work, and the ALS subset is valuable despite its small size.
The manuscript is generally clear about the high-level pipeline: EMG feature extraction, CTC prediction of HuBERT units, pretrained vocoder synthesis, and human transcription-based WER evaluation.

The covariance-based EMG representation and the comparison among vec(E), D(E), and spectrogram features are interesting. The result that full covariance features outperform spectrogram-style features is plausible and potentially useful.
The phoneme-guided auxiliary objective gives a measurable improvement in unit error rate, and the authors provide some ablations and implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main EMG-to-speech datasets contain only one healthy speaker and one ALS participant, so the paper does not establish generalization across speakers, sessions, electrode placements, disease stages, or day-to-day EMG non-stationarity.

The end-to-end performance remains weak: human-transcribed WER is about 62.6% on the healthy participant and 50.8% on the ALS participant. These results may be a useful starting point, but they do not convincingly support broad claims about functional speech restoration or practical neuroprosthetic communication.

The evaluation lacks strong direct baselines. The paper explains why prior systems are not directly comparable, but then the main experimental case rests mostly on internal feature ablations. There is no strong baseline such as an adapted EMG-to-phoneme/text pipeline, existing EMG-to-speech architectures under the same data conditions, or simpler transcript-conditioned alternatives.

The target speech units are derived from gTTS audio generated from transcripts rather than from participant speech, so the system is closer to EMG-to-discrete-linguistic-unit prediction plus off-the-shelf resynthesis than full speech synthesis from EMG. Claims about converting EMG “directly into audio” and capturing speech production mechanisms should be tempered accordingly.

The central linear-probing claim that self-supervised speech representations encode articulatory EMG structure is suggestive but not fully convincing. Important details and controls are missing, including how recorded audio and EMG are temporally aligned for probing, whether correlations survive temporal/permutation controls, and whether the result generalizes beyond the single healthy participant.

The gesture-clustering analysis is underdeveloped: the t-SNE visualization is from a single subject, the unsupervised clustering protocol is not sufficiently detailed, and the dismissal of spectrogram or rectified EMG as less comparable is not a substitute for a stronger discriminative baseline.

Reproducibility is only partially established. The paper promises code/data links, but the PDF itself contains placeholder-like project/data/github markers and no accessible details in the manuscript text. Several implementation choices, preprocessing steps, and target-construction choices would need to be fully released to make the work reproducible.

The clinical framing is overstated relative to the evidence. The ALS result uses one participant, one recording regime, and no longitudinal testing; the limitations acknowledge this, but the main narrative still leans heavily on clinical applicability.

The phoneme-guided decoding mechanism needs clearer separation of train/validation/test resources. The appendix reports a GRU mapping HuBERT units to phonemes with 0% PER and then uses it to estimate P(phoneme|unit), but it is not fully clear whether any test-set information leaks into the lookup or model-selection process.

Overall, the paper has a potentially useful dataset and some interesting modeling ideas, but unresolved concerns about evaluation rigor, scope of claims, baselines, and reproducibility prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: non-invasive EMG-to-speech synthesis, including a clinically relevant ALS demonstration. The framing is clearly relevant to speech/NLP and assistive communication.

The proposed dataset contribution is substantial: roughly 9 hours of large-vocabulary EMG speech data from a healthy participant, an ALS corpus, and an orofacial gesture dataset. If the code/data links are complete, this materially improves reproducibility in an area where prior work is often private.

The methodological idea of using covariance-based EMG representations and self-supervised speech units is well motivated. The paper gives useful empirical evidence that vec(E) outperforms spectrogram features and that phoneme-guided training improves HuBERT-unit decoding.

The paper is unusually transparent about limitations, including the single ALS participant, lack of longitudinal robustness analysis, and high residual WER. Appendices provide helpful implementation details, training losses, data-size ablations, and human evaluation protocols.

The evaluation uses several complementary metrics: UER, PER, WER from human transcription, MOS, and ablations over EMG representations and phoneme guidance. This supports the main technical contribution better than a single headline metric would.
weaknesses: The strongest scientific claims about self-supervised speech models implicitly encoding articulatory mechanisms are somewhat over-interpreted. A high linear correlation from S3 features to EMG power in one healthy speaker is suggestive, but not enough to establish a general mechanistic account; acoustic/phonetic confounds and subject specificity remain plausible explanations.

Generalization is a major limitation. The main speech datasets involve one healthy participant and one ALS participant, so the results do not yet show robustness across speakers, electrode placements, sessions, disease stages, or demographic variability. This is especially important for a non-invasive interface where day-to-day signal drift may be large.

End-to-end intelligibility remains modest: WER is around 62% for DATA_GENERAL and 51% for DATA_ALS. The paper is honest about this, but it limits the practical impact of the current system and makes the contribution stronger as a dataset/benchmark and proof of concept than as a mature speech prosthesis.

The comparison to prior work is necessarily indirect, but this still weakens the empirical case. Because the proposed task setting and data differ from prior EMG-to-speech and invasive BCI studies, it is hard to judge whether the method itself is competitive versus mainly benefiting from a new formulation and dataset.

Some evaluation choices need tighter justification. The phoneme-to-unit lookup construction may risk using broader corpus/test-distribution information unless the split discipline is made explicit, and the human transcription/MOS procedures would benefit from more detail on rater blinding, audio ordering, and whether raters heard any examples or references.

The synthesis pipeline depends heavily on pretrained gTTS-derived targets, HuBERT discretization, and a pretrained Tacotron vocoder. This is practical and reproducible, but it complicates attribution: improvements may reflect properties of the intermediate speech-unit system as much as EMG modeling advances.
